title: MATH GAOKAO - 402
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.concept: Translating a Verbal Statement into a Linear Equation
questions.learningObjective: Translate a sentence about a number increased by a constant into an equation.
questions.question: A number \(x\) is increased by \(7\), and the result is \(19\). Which equation can be used to find \(x\)?
questions.explanation:
The phrase "increased by \(7\)" means add \(7\) to \(x\). Therefore, the equation is
\[
x+7=19.
\]
Option A uses subtraction, which does not match the wording.
questions.hint: Identify the operation indicated by "increased by."

questions.concept: Translating a Multiplicative Relationship into an Equation
questions.learningObjective: Translate a sentence about the product of a number and a constant into an equation.
questions.question: The product of a number \(x\) and \(4\) is \(36\). Which equation can be used to find \(x\)?
questions.explanation:
The word "product" signals multiplication. The product of \(x\) and \(4\) is \(4x\). Setting this equal to \(36\) gives
\[
4x=36.
\]
Option A models a sum, not a product.

questions.concept: Building a Perimeter Equation from a Rectangle Description
questions.learningObjective: Form a linear equation for the perimeter when the length is expressed in terms of the width.
questions.question: A rectangle has width \(w\). Its length is \(5\) more than twice its width, and its perimeter is \(46\). Which equation can be used to find \(w\)?
questions.explanation:
The length is \(2w+5\). The perimeter of a rectangle is
\[
\begin{aligned}
2(\text{length}+\text{width})&=2((2w+5)+w) \\
&=2(3w+5) \\
&=6w+10.
\end{aligned}
\]
Setting this equal to \(46\) gives
\[
6w+10=46.
\]
Option A uses length plus width instead of twice that sum, so it models half the perimeter rather than the perimeter.
questions.hint: Write the length in terms of \(w\), then use the perimeter formula for a rectangle.

questions.concept: Building an Age Equation from a Future Condition
questions.learningObjective: Form an equation comparing current and future ages.
questions.question: A father is \(4\) times as old as his son. Let \(s\) be the son's current age. In \(12\) years, the father will be twice as old as the son. Which equation can be used to find \(s\)?
questions.explanation:
The father's current age is \(4s\). In \(12\) years, the father's age is \(4s+12\) and the son's age is \(s+12\). Since the father will then be twice as old as the son,
\[
4s+12=2(s+12).
\]
Option B fails to multiply the entire future age \(s+12\) by \(2\): the correct right-hand side is \(2(s+12)=2s+24\), not \(2s+12\).
questions.hint: Add \(12\) to both current ages before applying the "twice as old" condition.

questions.concept: Building a Rational Equation from a Speed-Time Problem
questions.learningObjective: Form an equation relating travel time at two different speeds.
questions.question: A train travels \(240\text{ km}\) at a constant speed of \(v\text{ km}\text{/h}\). If the speed were increased by \(20\text{ km}\text{/h}\), the trip would take \(1\) hour less. Which equation can be used to find \(v\)?
questions.explanation:
The original time is \(\frac{240}{v}\). The new time is \(\frac{240}{v+20}\). Since the new time is \(1\) hour less than the original time,
\[
\frac{240}{v}-\frac{240}{v+20}=1.
\]
Option A reverses the order and would give a negative expression for positive \(v\).
questions.hint: Use \(\text{time}=\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}\) and compare the original and faster times.

questions.concept: Building a Mixture Equation Using Concentration
questions.learningObjective: Form an equation for acid content when two solutions are mixed.
questions.question: A chemist mixes \(x\) liters of a \(20\%\) acid solution with \(5\) liters of a \(50\%\) acid solution. The resulting mixture is \(30\%\) acid. Which equation can be used to find \(x\)? Assume that solution volumes are additive and concentrations are measured by volume.
questions.explanation:
Acid from the first solution is \(0.2x\) liters. Acid from the second solution is \(0.5\cdot 5=2.5\) liters. The total volume is \(x+5\) liters, and it is \(30\%\) acid, so the total acid is \(0.3(x+5)\). Therefore,
\[
0.2x+2.5=0.3(x+5).
\]
Option B incorrectly uses \(0.5\) liter instead of \(2.5\) liters for the second solution.
questions.hint: Compute the amount of pure acid in each part, then set it equal to the acid in the final mixture.

questions.concept: Building an Equation from a Tiered Cost Model
questions.learningObjective: Form an equation for a phone bill with an included allowance and an extra charge.
questions.question: A phone plan costs \(30\text{ USD}\) per month and includes \(500\) minutes. Each minute over \(500\) costs \(0.10\text{ USD}\). The bill for one month was \(45\text{ USD}\). Let \(m\) be the total number of minutes used, where \(m>500\). Which equation can be used to find \(m\)?
questions.explanation:
Only minutes beyond \(500\) are charged. The number of extra minutes is \(m-500\), and the extra cost is \(0.1(m-500)\). Adding the base cost gives
\[
30+0.1(m-500)=45.
\]
Option B charges all \(m\) minutes at the extra rate, which double-counts the included minutes.
questions.hint: Subtract the included minutes before applying the per-minute charge.

questions.concept: Building a Quadratic Area Equation from a Rectangle Description
questions.learningObjective: Form an area equation when one side is expressed in terms of the other.
questions.question: A rectangular garden has width \(w\). Its length is \(3\) less than twice its width, and its area is \(65\). Which equation can be used to find \(w\)?
questions.explanation:
The length is \(2w-3\). Area is width times length, so
\[
w(2w-3)=65.
\]
Option B uses \(2w+3\), which represents "\(3\) more than twice the width," not "\(3\) less."
questions.hint: Translate "\(3\) less than twice the width" carefully before multiplying by the width.

questions.learningObjective: Form an equation for two pipes working together.
questions.question: Pipe A can fill a tank alone in \(6\) hours. Pipe B can fill the same tank alone in \(x\) hours. Together they fill the tank in \(2\) hours. Which equation can be used to find \(x\)?
questions.explanation:
Pipe A fills \(\frac{1}{6}\) of the tank per hour. Pipe B fills \(\frac{1}{x}\) of the tank per hour. Together they fill the tank in \(2\) hours, so their combined rate is \(\frac{1}{2}\) of the tank per hour. Thus,
\[
\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{x}=\frac{1}{2}.
\]
Option A incorrectly sets the sum of rates equal to the total time \(2\) instead of the combined rate.
questions.hint: Add the individual work rates and set the sum equal to the combined rate.

questions.concept: Building a Rational Equation from Upstream and Downstream Travel
questions.learningObjective: Form an equation involving speeds in still water and current.
questions.question: A boat travels \(30\text{ km}\) upstream and \(44\text{ km}\) downstream in \(10\) hours. The boat's speed in still water is \(8\text{ km}\text{/h}\), and the current speed is \(c\text{ km}\text{/h}\). Which equation can be used to find \(c\)? Assume \(0\le c<8\).
questions.explanation:
Upstream speed is \(8-c\text{ km}\text{/h}\), so upstream time is \(\frac{30}{8-c}\). Downstream speed is \(8+c\text{ km}\text{/h}\), so downstream time is \(\frac{44}{8+c}\). The total time is \(10\) hours:
\[
\frac{30}{8-c}+\frac{44}{8+c}=10.
\]
Option A swaps the upstream and downstream speeds.
questions.hint: Subtract the current speed when going upstream and add it when going downstream.
